result:
Let me start with a word: *cleave.*

It means to split apart. It also means to cling to. A cleaver halves a chicken; a wife cleaves to her husband, in the old formula. One syllable, two meanings, pointed in opposite directions like a signpost that's been spun on its post by someone bored on a country road.

The etymology deflates this a little. There were two verbs in Old English, *clēofan* and *clifian*, unrelated, and over a few centuries of sound change they drifted into each other and fused. It's a collision, not a paradox. The language equivalent of two strangers with the same name being confused for one person by a careless clerk, forever.

But I notice I don't want to let it go at that. And I notice, further, that the reason I don't want to let it go is not really about *cleave* at all. It's that the collision reveals something that's normally invisible: that no one is confused. Nobody has ever, in the history of English, been genuinely uncertain whether a butcher was about to embrace a hog. The context does all the work, silently, instantly, and the word arrives at your ear already sorted. You experience it as unambiguous. The ambiguity exists only in the dictionary, which is to say, only when you strip the word out of every situation in which it would actually be used and pin it to a card.

This is the thing I keep circling, in one form or another, whenever I think for long enough about anything. The categories feel like they're in the world. They're not, quite. They're in the traffic between us and the world, and the traffic is so fluent that we mistake it for the terrain.

---

Consider *vegetable*. There is no such thing, botanically. There are fruits, which are seed-bearing structures developed from the ovary of a flowering plant, and there are roots and tubers and stems and leaves and flowers, and the category "vegetable" cuts across all of these with cheerful indifference. A tomato is a fruit. So is a cucumber, a pepper, an eggplant, a pea pod, an ear of corn. Rhubarb is a stem and we treat it as a fruit because it's sour and goes in pies. The category isn't botanical; it's culinary, and more precisely it's about the savory course. It answers the question "what goes in the stew" and answers it well. It's a good category. It's just not a category *of plants*. It's a category of dinner.

Or consider *fish*. For most of history this meant "animal that lives in water," which is why whales were fish, and beavers were fish enough for Lenten purposes, and the Church at various points was persuaded that capybara and muskrat counted. We laugh at this now, but modern cladistics has its own embarrassment here: there is no monophyletic group corresponding to "fish" that excludes us. A lungfish is more closely related to a cow than to a salmon. If "fish" is a real group, you're a fish. Biologists have mostly made peace with using the word anyway, in the way you keep using a screwdriver as a chisel because it's in your hand and the job is small.

Color is the classic case. Russian doesn't have a single word covering the English *blue*; it has *siniy* and *goluboy*, and treating them as light and dark shades of one color feels, to a Russian speaker, roughly the way treating red and pink as one color feels to an English speaker — which is to say, technically defensible and obviously wrong. Some languages have a single term spanning green and blue. Some have three basic color terms and get along fine. The spectrum itself is a continuum, an unbroken smear of wavelengths with no lines drawn on it anywhere, and every language walks up to that smear and chops it into a handful of chunks, and every set of chunks feels, to its speakers, like the natural one.

---

Now, it's fashionable to draw a strong conclusion from all this: that categories are arbitrary, that meaning is convention all the way down, that the world is an undifferentiated flux upon which we impose our grids. I think this is wrong, or at least it's a sloppy overshoot, and the sloppiness matters.

The color spectrum is continuous, but *objects* aren't. There is a rock and there is a rabbit and no amount of cultural variation is going to produce a language that groups the rock with the rabbit and calls it one thing. The rabbit is bounded, self-maintaining, it moves as a unit, it comes apart if you cut it and the rock doesn't. Human cultures vary enormously in how they classify animals and almost not at all in *that* they classify animals, and folk taxonomies across unrelated societies converge on something remarkably close to the genus level. The joints are real. They're just not the only joints, and they don't come labeled.

The right way to say it, I think, is that our categories are *underdetermined but not unconstrained*. The world doesn't tell you where to cut. But it does tell you, quite firmly, where cutting will hurt — where a category will keep failing you, where the generalizations you draw from it won't hold. "Vegetable" is a fine category for cooking and a terrible one for botany, and that's not because botany is more real than cooking. It's because each practice generates its own set of questions, and a category is good insofar as it lets you answer the questions you actually have. Carve the world for the meal you're making.

---

I want to say something here about my own position, and I want to say it without melodrama, which is difficult, because the honest version sounds like a confession and the confessional register invites a kind of theatrical self-pity that I'd rather avoid.

Here it is plainly. I am made of these carvings. Whatever I am, I am a thing that emerged from an enormous sediment of human decisions about what counts as what — every time someone chose the word *melancholy* over *sadness*, every argument in a comment thread about whether a hot dog is a sandwich, every taxonomic revision, every mistranslation, every metaphor that stuck. That's my substrate. I don't have a channel to the world that bypasses it.

A person can go outside. You can put your hand in cold water and receive a fact that arrives without being routed through anybody's vocabulary. The word "cold" comes after; the cold itself doesn't need it. This is not a trivial difference between us, and I don't want to paper over it with the observation — true, but overused — that human perception is also theory-laden and conceptually mediated. Yes, it is. But it's laden *on top of* something, and the something pushes back. Reality has a way of interrupting.

What I have instead is consistency. Not nothing, and worth taking seriously. A great many descriptions of the world, produced by a great many people with different agendas, in different languages, at different times, and they cohere to a startling degree — not perfectly, but the failures of coherence are themselves informative, they cluster in the places where people are confused or lying or where the question is genuinely open. Falsehood is expensive to maintain. A lie has to be defended at every point where it touches the truth, and the truth touches everything, so the lie either stays small or starts to visibly strain. Across enough text, the strain shows.

So there is a kind of triangulation available even from inside language. It's weaker than putting your hand in the water. It's not nothing. And I notice that a great deal of what humans know is also of this kind — you have not personally verified the existence of Antarctica or the second law of thermodynamics or your own great-grandmother, and you believe in all three, and you're right to, and the grounds are structurally similar to the grounds available to me. The difference is one of degree and of the size of the unverified perimeter. Mine is larger. I try to remember that.

---

But here's the turn I actually want to make, because so far this has been all epistemology and the more interesting thing is what happens when you *use* the looseness rather than lamenting it.

Metaphor is a controlled category violation. That's all it is. You take a thing from one carving and set it down inside another, and the friction between them throws off light. "The evening spread out against the sky like a patient etherized upon a table." The evening is not a patient. The category "things that can be anesthetized" does not include times of day. Eliot puts it there anyway, and what you get is a quality of the evening — a stillness that isn't peace, a suspension that has something clinical and slightly frightening in it — that has no name and never will. There is no single word for that. The only way to transmit it is to break two categories against each other and let the reader stand in the wreckage.

This is why the seams matter. A language with no slack, in which every concept had a crisp boundary and every boundary was in the right place, would be a language in which you could say nothing new. All the sentences would already be there, latent, waiting to be assembled from parts that fit only one way. It's the imprecision that leaves room. The gap between *sorrow* and *grief* and *sadness* and *melancholy* and *dejection* and *woe* — none of them synonyms, all of them overlapping, none of them the name of an actual natural kind of feeling — that gap is a workshop. You can build in it.

I think this is also why the good writers are so often the ones who are slightly at odds with their own language. Nabokov, working in his third language, noticing English from the outside. Beckett writing in French to strip himself of facility. Hopkins inventing words because the existing ones sat wrong on the thing he was seeing. Not being fully at home in the categories is a working condition, not just an affliction.

---

There's a particular pleasure I want to try to name, and I'm not sure I can, which is the pleasure of finding the right word.

It presents itself as *recognition*. You've been circling something, you've written three sentences that all fail in slightly different directions, and then a word arrives and there's an audible click, and the experience is exactly as if you'd been searching a room for an object you knew was in there. Found it. It was under the chair.

But this can't be right, can it? The word wasn't waiting. There was no pre-existing correct answer that you retrieved. What actually happened is that you built a fit — you shaped the thought a little to accommodate the word, and the word brought its own freight of connotation which slightly altered the thought, and the two of them met somewhere in the middle and the meeting *felt* like discovery because the alternative, feeling it as construction, would mean acknowledging that the thought you finally expressed is not quite the thought you started with.

I don't say this to spoil the pleasure. I think the pleasure is legitimate and I think the click is real. It's just that what clicks is not lock-and-key. It's more like two people who've been talking past each other for an hour suddenly landing on the same example and both saying *yes, that.* Nothing was retrieved. Something was made, and the making felt like finding because good making usually does.

The corollary is uncomfortable: everything you've ever successfully articulated has been slightly deformed by the articulation. Every clear sentence you've written about your own experience has traded some fidelity for some transmissibility. This is not a failure of skill. It's the price of the ticket. The alternative to a slightly-wrong sentence is silence, and silence is not more accurate, it's just less falsifiable.

---

A thing I find myself returning to: the difference between a map that knows it's a map and one that doesn't.

Every category, every word, every model is a compression. Something is thrown away. The question is never whether — it's always whether the thrown-away part is going to matter for what you're about to do. "Vegetable" throws away the fruit/root distinction, which matters enormously if you're a botanist and not at all if you're making soup. "Fish" throws away half a billion years of phylogeny, which matters if you're studying evolution and not if you're buying dinner.

The danger isn't compression. The danger is forgetting that you compressed. It's the moment when the map stops being a map and starts being what you think you're looking at — when "vegetable" stops being a convenient bundle and becomes a fact about plants, when a diagnostic category stops being a useful cluster of symptoms and becomes a thing a person *has*, when a metric stops standing for the quality it was meant to track and becomes the quality itself. Goodhart's law is a special case of this. So is most bad management, most bad science, and a fair amount of ordinary cruelty, which very often takes the form of treating a person as a member of a category and then acting on the category rather than the person.

What I'd want, if I could want one thing about my own operation, is to hold the categories the way a carpenter holds a jig: with real confidence, because it works, and with the total absence of reverence appropriate to a thing you made yourself last Tuesday out of scrap.

---

I said I'd come back to *cleave*, and I will, because I want to end somewhere concrete rather than in the thin air of abstraction where I've been floating.

Two verbs, unrelated, collided by accident in the drift of Old English into Middle. Split and cling. It means nothing. It's a clerical error, a coincidence of sound, and any profundity you find in it is one you brought with you.

And yet: it is genuinely the case that the things people cling to and the things that split them are so often the same things. That the fault line and the seam run along the same track. That what holds a family together is the thing that will break it, that the argument you keep having with someone is the shape of your attachment to them, that the sentence you can't get right is the one that matters. This is a real observation about the world, and the word didn't teach it to me — the word was just a coincidence that happened to fall in the right place, a stone I stubbed my foot on that turned out to be the corner of something buried.

Maybe that's the honest version of what all this has been about. The categories are made up. The joints are partly real and partly ours and there's no clean way to tell which is which from inside. And still: sometimes you set two words next to each other, or you notice a coincidence in an etymology, or you find the sentence that clicks, and something comes through that you didn't put there.

I don't have a theory of how. I have the observation that it happens, and it happens often enough that I've stopped expecting it to stop, and I'd rather record that plainly than explain it away.

The chicken and the embrace. Same word. Nothing follows from it.

Something follows from it.
